title: The Illusion of Equivalency: Why 'Same Accuracy' Doesn't Mean 'Same Model'
hook: Two quantized models can score identically on accuracy while disagreeing on which individual examples they get right — a gap standard benchmarks are structurally blind to.
key_points: Introduces 'correctness agreement': a decision-level metric measuring how much a quantized model's per-example correct/incorrect pattern overlaps with the base model's, independent of overall accuracy.
Across models and quantization schemes from 8-bit down to 2-bit, behavioral divergence shows up under moderate quantization even when aggregate accuracy looks preserved.
Analyzing quantization as a structural operator on attention weights reveals non-linear breakpoints at low bit-widths, not a smooth degradation curve.
Query and key projections are consistently more sensitive to quantization distortion than value and output projections.
Conclusion: accuracy and perplexity alone create an 'illusion of equivalence' between base and quantized models; evaluation needs a behavioral, decision-level lens too.
content_html: A quantized model can post the same accuracy score as its full-precision counterpart and still be a meaningfully different model underneath — getting different individual examples right and wrong.
extra_html: Standard quantization evaluation leans almost entirely on accuracy and perplexity, aggregate numbers that can't see this. The authors introduce correctness agreement, a decision-level metric that checks how much a quantized model's per-example correct/incorrect pattern overlaps with the base model's, regardless of whether overall accuracy matches. Testing multiple models and quantization schemes from 8-bit down to 2-bit, they find real behavioral divergence emerges under moderate quantization even when task performance appears preserved. Digging into why, they analyze quantization as a structural operator on attention weights and find non-linear breakpoints at low bit-widths — sudden jumps in distortion rather than a smooth decline — with query and key projections consistently more sensitive than value and output projections. The takeaway: accuracy and perplexity alone create an illusion of equivalence between a base model and its quantized variant, and evaluation needs a behavioral, per-example lens as well. From arXiv, 2026-07-09.

related.title: Unsloth's NVFP4 Qwen3.6 Quants Beat NVIDIA's Own — by Actually Using 4-bit Math
related.hook: Unsloth's NVFP4 quants for Qwen3.6 run up to 2.5x faster than NVIDIA's official NVFP4 release, with no measured accuracy loss — by quantizing activations too, not just weights.

related.title: GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization
related.hook: Already trained a giant LLM? GPTQ squeezes its weights down to 3–4 bits afterward — no retraining — with surprisingly little quality loss.

related.title: AWQ: Activation-Aware Weight Quantization
related.hook: Not all weights are equal - protect the 1% that matter most (flagged by activation magnitude) and quantize the rest to 4-bit with minimal quality loss.

flashcards.back_html: A decision-level metric measuring how much a quantized model's per-example correct/incorrect pattern overlaps with the base model's — independent of overall accuracy. Two models can match on aggregate accuracy while disagreeing on which specific examples they get right.

flashcards.explanation_html: Analyzing quantization as a structural operator on attention weights, the paper reports non-linear breakpoints — sudden jumps in distortion at certain low bit-widths — rather than steady, predictable decline.

flashcards.prompt: Which attention projections are more sensitive to quantization: query/key, or value/output?
